title: Diwali: the row of lamps
hook: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri: nine forms of the Goddess, and so many ways to keep the nights. Your line was nine nights, then the dawn. Today, Diwali one more time, and the story the south tells. Day ninety-five.

In Chennai or Bangalore, Diwali starts in the dark, hours before sunrise. The house is still asleep. Someone's grandmother is already up, warming sesame oil. Everyone gets woken, grumbling, for a special oil bath before dawn, then new clothes, then the first firecrackers, crackling while the sky is still black. Ask a child in the north why the lamps are lit, and the answer is often Rama coming home. Ask a child in Chennai why the whole house is up before dawn, and a different name comes up: Narakasura. And a different hero. Two of them, actually.
screen: `UP BEFORE DAWN.` → `AN OIL BATH IN THE DARK.` → `A DIFFERENT STORY.`

segments.voice: Narakasura was a demon king who grew so powerful he terrorized heaven and earth. The Bhagavata Purana tells how he stole the earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods, and held thousands of young women captive in his fortress. Krishna goes to face him, riding the great bird Garuda, and with him goes his wife Satyabhama. In many tellings, especially in the south, it's Satyabhama who strikes the final blow. And the story told at Diwali adds one more thing. As Narakasura dies, he asks for something: let the day of my death be remembered not with mourning, but with lights. So, tradition says, the day before the new moon became Naraka Chaturdashi, the fourteenth day of Naraka, and in much of south India that pre-dawn morning is the heart of Diwali. Many families say the oil bath before dawn washes off the dark. And then, released captives, returned earrings, a whole world let out of a fortress, and lamps lit. Rama coming home, Lakshmi at the open door, Narakasura's last wish. Different regions, one row of lamps. And neighbors light lamps on the same nights for their own reasons. Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas, remembering Guru Hargobind's release from prison. Jains remember the night Mahavira attained liberation. Every one of those stories is about someone getting out, or coming home. Light the way home.
screen: `NARAKASURA HOLDS THE WORLD CAPTIVE.` · `SATYABHAMA STRIKES THE BLOW.` · `REMEMBER ME WITH LIGHTS.` · `ONE ROW OF LAMPS, MANY STORIES.` · then, large: `LIGHT THE WAY HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light one light, and think of who you'd guide home. If you can, light a candle, or picture one. Breathe. Think this time of someone who is stuck. Not far away, but trapped: in a job, an illness, a bad stretch, a fortress of their own. Picture your small light at the door of that fortress. You can't break the walls. You can show them where the door is. Hold that picture. The bell holds the time.
Diwali. A row of lamps, lit in the north for Rama's return, in the south for a world let out of Narakasura's fortress.
Your line: light the way home. Today, do one small thing for someone who feels stuck: a call, a meal, a ride, a door held open. Day ninety-five.

howItsDone: In much of south India, Diwali centers on Naraka Chaturdashi: families rise before dawn for an oil bath, wear new clothes, light lamps and firecrackers, and share sweets, remembering Krishna and Satyabhama's victory over Narakasura.

original.note: Sanskrit: the fourteenth day of Naraka, the morning before Diwali's new moon.

trapdoor: what you thought: Diwali has one story.
what it means: one row of lamps holds many stories of getting out or coming home: Rama, Lakshmi, a world freed from Narakasura.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata Purana 10.59 tells Naraka's defeat; the dying wish for lights and Satyabhama's final blow come from later and regional tellings.

sources.ref: Bandi Chhor Divas (Sikh) and Mahavira's nirvana (Jain) on Diwali

notes: Bhagavata 10.59: Krishna and Satyabhama ride Garuda; Krishna kills Naraka (Bhauma) with the discus; 16,100 captive women released; Aditi's earrings returned. Satyabhama striking the final blow is from later/regional tellings (e.g. some Puranic variants, Telugu and Tamil traditions). Framed as 'in many tellings'. Confirm.
Narakasura's dying wish for lights: popular tradition; framed as 'the story told at Diwali'. Confirm.

Sikh and Jain neighbors mentioned briefly as sharing the night, without comparison. Bandi Chhor Divas: Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior Fort. Jain: Mahavira's nirvana at Pavapuri. Confirm wording is acceptable to those paths.
Pre-dawn oil bath (Ganga snanam) on Naraka Chaturdashi, especially Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the hook no longer has the narrator say 'why we light lamps' (the narrator is never a member of the faith) and drops the unsourced 'four in the morning'; Naraka Chaturdashi's origin and the oil bath's meaning are now framed as what tradition and families say.
